newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Speculation mounts Mercedes head may quit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Speculation mounts Mercedes head may quit.

text.p: Speculation the head of German carmaker Mercedes-Benz AG, Helmut Werner, may step down intensified on Tuesday, raising the prospect of what could be a serious loss to the company.

Although Mercedes denied reports that any decision had been made, the German media was rife with reports that Mercedes chairman Werner could leave by the end of the year, the loser in a fight over the reorganisation of parent company, Daimler-Benz.
Industry analysts, some of whom also believe Werner may go, said his loss would be a blow to Mercedes which he has guided back to profitability with a massive overhaul in model strategy.
"It would be negative for Mercedes if Werner was to go," said Sabine Bluemel, analyst at IMI Sigeco. "He has turned Mercedes around."
Speculation that Werner may be ready to quit reached a new level on Tuesday with the Handelsblatt newspaper reporting that he had already prepared a letter of resignation -- a report Werner denied.
Rumours have been circulating for several weeks that Werner may be drafted in by Volkswagen to help solve its legal battle with U.S. based General Motors over allegations of industrial espionage.
Although analysts give the Volkswagen report little credence, there was an increasing belief in the investment community that talk of Werner's departure was not far off the mark.

The debate about Werner's future at Mercedes stem from the plans of Daimler-Benz chairman Juergen Schrempp to reorganise Daimler, bringing the Mercedes unit more tightly into the group structure and making it less independent.

Werner, whose unit is responsible for the bulk of sales at Daimler, has been reported to be bitterly opposed to the plans, dismissing offers from Schrempp of important jobs in the new group struture and threatening to resign.
Analysts said the loss of Werner, the architect of the most sweeping shift in Mercedes' corporate strategy, would be a blow to the company just as it reaches strong profit growth.

"The financial markets have so far welcomed Daimler's restructuring. But if out of this came Werner's departure, there would be negative threat," said John Lawson, analyst at Salmon Brothers in London.

Werner took over at Mercedes in 1993 when it was deep in the red. By cutting costs and pushing through a broad swathe of new models, he has transformed Mercedes into one of the most profitable carmakers in the world.

In 1995, Mercedes made 2.28 billion marks ($1.47 billion), selling 583,432 cars. Werner believes that by pushing into new markets with cars such as the tiny A-Class next year and the sporty SLK roadster, he can boost sales to more than a million vehicles within five years.
"Widening the product range was a cunning, clever move for Mercedes," said Peter Schmidt, analyst at Automotive Industry Data outside London.

Analysts agreed that through his aggressive direction of Mercedes, Werner has won a following in the investment community that would not quickly be replaced and that Daimler's share price could sag on any resignation announcement.

Should Werner indeed leave, most expect Mercedes to look outside the Daimler group for a replacement. But few names have surfaced so far and some analysts said it may be hard for Daimler to find a solid candidate.
Under the new structure, Schrempp will play a much closer role in Mercedes' automotive business, giving any new car chief less room to carry out his own ideas.
Most analysts agreed, however, the basic strategy laid down by Werner would remain in place. Demand for the SLK has been strong and analysts also see solid advance sales for the A-Class.

Some, however, think that Schrempp is less committed to the Smart Car joint venture Mercedes has with the Swiss SMH Swatch group to produce an ultra small two-seat car. Daimler's withdrawl from that project could not be ruled out if Werner were to leave.
